claims.text: Dealloying a precursor alloy can produce HEA three-dimensional nanoframeworks.
Dealloying selectively dissolves less noble components from the precursor alloy.
Selective dissolution leaves an interconnected noble-metal skeleton.
The proposed precursor is a near-homogeneous multicomponent mixture containing both noble metals and less noble elements.
Exposure to an acidic or alkaline corrosive environment selectively dissolves the less noble elements.
Controlling electrochemical potential, temperature, and solution concentration can promote uniform removal of less noble constituents.
Selective removal causes a percolative collapse of the initial solid-solution structure.
This structural transformation produces a porous three-dimensional network of interconnected noble-metal-rich regions.
Removal of less noble elements induces surface restructuring.
The remaining noble metals reorganize to minimize surface energy.
Surface-energy-driven reorganization forms a highly porous, interconnected nanoframework.
The resulting nanoframework has a larger specific surface area.
The resulting three-dimensional porous nanoframework has more accessible active sites.
The dealloyed nanoframework should exhibit better catalytic performance than a non-structured HEA.
A sufficiently large difference in dissolution kinetics between noble and less noble elements is required for effective nanoframework formation.
Concurrent dissolution of noble and less noble elements may suppress nanoframework formation.
